title: How to Keep a Remote Cold Calling Team Fired Up (When Nobody Ever Meets in Person)
summary: Vangates co-founder Michael Ewald shares eight ways to keep a remote cold calling team motivated, improve performance, and turn more conversations into meetings.
body_markdown:
Cold calling is one of the most demanding jobs in sales. Rejection is constant, results can be unpredictable, and maintaining a high level of energy throughout the day requires considerable discipline.


Now imagine doing all of that alone, sitting at home, without colleagues around you, without a sales floor buzzing with activity, and without anyone to celebrate with when you finally book that hard-earned meeting.


That’s the reality of managing a fully remote cold calling team.


At Vangates, we operate a remote calling team with 23 seats. Most of our callers have never met each other in person. Yet we’ve managed to build a competitive, performance-driven environment where people genuinely enjoy being part of the team.


Before co-founding[Vangates](https://vangates.com/?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) , I spent ten years cold calling myself. That experience taught me something important: **Successful cold calling isn’t just about motivation. It’s about building a system that consistently produces, measures, and improves performance.**


Here are eight principles we’ve developed along the way.


## **1. Track Everything. And I Mean Everything.**


Most sales organizations track[a handful of KPIs](https://close.com/blog/sales-kpis-metrics?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) : calls made, conversations held, and meetings booked.


That’s a starting point, but it’s nowhere near enough.


At Vangates, our goal is to measure the entire employee journey, from the moment someone logs into the CRM to the eventual outcome of the opportunities they generate.


We track metrics such as:


- CRM login times and working activity
- Dials and conversations per hour
- Time between calls and inactive periods
- Emails sent and other outreach activities
- Conversation duration
- Meetings booked and meetings attended
- [Conversion rates between individual stages](https://close.com/blog/cold-calling-conversion-funnel-analytics?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study)
- Downstream outcomes of the opportunities generated


Why go into this level of detail?


**Because** **every measurable step in a process represents a potential opportunity for improvement.**


If one caller consistently books more meetings than another, I don’t just want to know that they’re performing better. I want to understand why.


Are they having more conversations? Are their conversations longer? Do they convert more conversations into meetings? Are they working more consistently throughout the day?


Once we identify the relevant differences, we can investigate what’s driving them and determine whether those behaviors can be replicated across the team.


**The principle is simple: If you want to improve performance systematically, you need to understand the process behind the results.**


## **2. Build a Recruiting Funnel That Gets Smarter With Every Hire**


Hiring the wrong people is expensive. In a remote calling environment, it’s particularly damaging.


At Vangates, we generally look for two profiles: ambitious people early in their careers who want to prove themselves, and experienced callers who deliberately choose remote work.


But regardless of their background, candidates need to demonstrate that they can actually do the job.


- **Give candidates a realistic calling assessment.** We provide candidates with a business case and ask them to prepare and[conduct test calls](https://close.com/blog/sales-hiring-101-for-startups?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) . Crucially, we don’t explain every detail beforehand. We want to understand how quickly someone grasps a new business model, how independently they prepare, and how they approach an unfamiliar situation. Their preparation tells us almost as much as their performance during the calls.
- **Introduce realistic trial working days.** If you’re hiring someone for a full-time calling position, have them work at least two realistic full working days. Observe their activity, consistency, adaptability, and development. One pattern we’ve repeatedly observed is particularly revealing:


- Strong candidates tend to improve on the second day. They become more familiar with the case, adjust their approach, and gain confidence.
- Weak candidates often move in the opposite direction. Their activity drops, their energy declines, and their initial enthusiasm disappears. If someone is already struggling to maintain motivation during the trial phase, that’s a serious warning sign.


- **Measure the effectiveness of your assessment itself.** This is where recruiting becomes a continuous optimization process. Track assessment results, trial-day performance, and subsequent employee performance. Then compare them. Which candidates eventually became top performers? Which hires didn’t work out? Were there warning signs during the assessment that you overlooked? Use these findings to refine your selection criteria.


**The goal isn’t to hire more people. It’s to become better at identifying the people who will succeed.**


## **3. Create Structure Without Turning Remote Work Into Surveillance**


One of the biggest challenges of remote work is isolation.


Without deliberate communication structures, employees can gradually become disconnected from their colleagues and the organization.


And different personalities respond to that environment very differently.


- Some people are highly conscientious and intrinsically motivated. They maintain their performance even when nobody is watching.
- Others struggle with the lack of external structure. Their activity gradually declines, often before anyone notices a serious problem.


That’s why[remote leadership](https://close.com/blog/manage-remote-sales-teams?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) requires both communication and transparency.


My preferred approach is to offer daily opportunities for interaction without making every meeting mandatory.


- Employees should have the option to join a daily check-in, ask questions, discuss challenges, or simply connect with colleagues.
- **Once a week, the entire team should come together.** That meeting needs a clear structure and purpose. It should create alignment, provide opportunities for shared learning, and strengthen the sense of belonging.
- Beyond group meetings, regular one-on-one conversations are essential.


**Performance dashboards can tell you what someone is doing. They can’t always tell you why.**


Sometimes an employee needs additional training. Sometimes they’re frustrated with a campaign. Sometimes something outside work is affecting their performance.


You won’t discover those things by looking at a spreadsheet.


## **4. Celebrate Every Single Success**


In a physical sales office, someone books a meeting, rings a bell, and everyone notices.


In a remote environment, that moment can disappear completely.


Unless you deliberately make it visible.


- At Vangates, every booked meeting gets celebrated in Slack. A GIF gets posted, the employee is mentioned by name, and the achievement becomes visible to the team.
- Weekly and monthly results should be communicated openly. People should know what the team has accomplished, who contributed, and what progress has been made.


It sounds simple because it is. But small, immediate moments of recognition matter, particularly in a job where rejection is part of everyday life.


**Success needs visibility. Otherwise, remote work can turn even exceptional performance into an isolated experience.**


## **5. Make Competition Part of Your Culture**


Sales is competitive by nature.


And in my experience, many of the people who genuinely excel at cold calling have a competitive streak.


They enjoy comparing results, pushing their limits, and proving that they can outperform yesterday’s numbers or their colleagues.


Not every excellent caller needs competition to stay motivated. But for those who do, it can be an incredibly powerful driver.


So use it.


- We recognize top performers on a weekly and monthly basis, and[performance rankings remain visible](https://close.com/blog/sales-leaderboard?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) through our dashboards.
- When someone becomes the top performer of the week, recognize them in the team’s communication channels. When someone wins the month, make sure the wider organization knows.
- [Reward those achievements](https://close.com/blog/sales-incentives?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) . The rewards don’t necessarily need to be expensive. Often, the recognition and the satisfaction of winning matter more than the financial value itself.


**What matters is creating a tangible distinction between average and exceptional performance.**


Of course, leaderboards also reveal the other end of the spectrum.


Employees who consistently rank near the bottom receive a clear signal that improvement is necessary.


That doesn’t mean publicly humiliating anyone. It means creating transparency around expectations and performance.


And it leads directly to the next principle.


## **6. Coach the Middle, Challenge the Bottom, and Raise the Standard**


A performance-driven environment needs more than rankings.


It needs a clear approach to developing employees.


When someone underperforms, the first question shouldn’t be whether to replace them.


It should be: **Why are they underperforming, and can we change it?**


This is where detailed KPI tracking becomes invaluable.


- **If someone makes fewer calls than their colleagues,** the problem might be activity, workflow, or discipline.
- **If they generate plenty of conversations but rarely book meetings,** the problem is more likely related to their sales technique.
- **If their conversations consistently end after a few seconds,** we might need to examine their opening, tonality, or ability to establish relevance.


Different problems require different interventions.


We’ve seen this firsthand when introducing[Predictive Dialer](https://close.com/calling?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) technology. Experienced callers often adapted immediately and appreciated the increased pace. Less experienced callers sometimes struggled to convert the additional conversations into meetings.


That told us where to[focus our coaching](https://close.com/blog/sales-coaching?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) :[opening techniques](https://close.com/blog/cold-call-opening-lines?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) , tonality, and the ability to handle conversations effectively. But there’s another side to this.


**Coaching is management’s responsibility. Improvement is a shared responsibility.**


Employees must actively engage with feedback, practice their skills, and take ownership of their development. You can provide excellent training, but you cannot force someone to become better.


If performance remains consistently below expectations despite appropriate support, you eventually need to make a decision.


Maintaining high standards is essential, not just for productivity but also for the motivation of the people who consistently deliver.


## **7. Let Technology Eliminate the Grind**


You cannot scale a calling operation efficiently by adding headcount alone.


At some point, better processes and technology become significantly more valuable than simply hiring additional callers.


Our philosophy is straightforward: **Let technology handle repetitive tasks so people can focus on conversations.**


At Vangates, we use Close to structure and manage our calling operations.


[Smart Views](https://close.com/crm?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) provide callers with automatically updated lead lists, eliminating unnecessary time spent deciding whom to contact next.


For high-volume campaigns, we use the Predictive Dialer. Instead of manually dialing one number after another and waiting for someone to answer, the system calls multiple leads and connects available callers when a person picks up.


The impact on our operations has been substantial. After implementing Predictive Dialer technology,[we observed](https://close.com/customers/vangates?utm_source=close-blog&utm_medium=organic-social&utm_campaign=vangates-case-study) :


- **109% more dials per hour**
- **43% more conversations per hour**
- **21–70% more meetings booked** , depending on the individual caller


These are results from our own implementation, not guaranteed outcomes for every team.


The tool creates additional opportunities. The quality of your people and processes determines how effectively those opportunities are converted.


## **8. Accept Turnover. Then Turn It Into an Advantage.**


Let’s address something many managers prefer not to discuss. Cold calling has a naturally high potential for employee turnover. And even an excellent recruiting process won’t eliminate it.


Especially when hiring younger people or candidates who haven’t previously worked in cold calling, you’ll encounter individuals who discover that the job simply isn’t for them.


Some initially believe they can handle constant rejection but eventually realize how emotionally demanding it can be. Others respond differently.


They recognize that dealing with rejection is a skill they can develop. They see cold calling as an opportunity to strengthen their confidence, communication abilities, and resilience.


When someone realizes the role isn’t right for them, it’s often better for both sides to acknowledge that early.


Otherwise, motivation declines, performance deteriorates, and the situation becomes increasingly frustrating.


**This is why recruiting needs to be a permanent process, not an emergency response to employee departures.**


You should always be building your pipeline of potential candidates. But there’s another dimension to turnover that I find particularly interesting. Long-term employees bring stability, experience, and strong relationships. Those are valuable advantages.


However, teams that never change can also become comfortable with existing standards.


New employees introduce different perspectives, fresh energy, and sometimes capabilities that exceed those of existing team members.


If your recruiting assessment continuously improves, your incoming hires should become progressively stronger.


And when that happens, the performance benchmark for the entire team rises.


Someone who was considered an excellent performer a year ago might suddenly find themselves in the middle of the leaderboard.


That’s not necessarily because they’ve become worse. It’s because the standard has improved. This creates a continuous cycle:


- Better recruiting produces stronger employees.
- Stronger employees establish higher benchmarks.
- Higher benchmarks reveal new opportunities for improvement.
- Those insights help refine recruiting and coaching even further.


Over time, the organization becomes more capable. **Even employees who eventually leave can benefit enormously from the experience.**


Some discover that cold calling isn’t the right career path for them. Others leave with significantly stronger communication skills, greater confidence, and a much better understanding of sales.


We’ve seen former callers move into other sales positions after developing their foundations with us.


Cold calling can be an incredibly demanding training ground.


Not everyone will stay. But many will leave having learned skills that benefit them throughout their careers.


## **The Real Secret: Build a System That Makes People Better**


Managing a remote cold calling team isn’t about finding one motivational trick that keeps everyone excited.


It’s about creating an environment where motivation, accountability, development, and performance reinforce each other.


The objective isn’t to build a team where nobody ever leaves.


**The objective is to build a team where the people who stay continuously improve, the people who join raise the standard, and even those who leave gain something valuable from the experience.**


That’s how you build a remote calling operation that doesn’t just maintain performance but gets better over time.
